speechtext:
While I think the
Liberal party has lost its greatest asset in his retirement, still it is a good thing for

Canada that he has gone. If the amount had been five cents, that is about his size, and I think he would have taken it. However, I am not here to discuss that. From the time the Minister of Railways put thai man in charge of the Government Railways he has done nothing but make trouble, and whenever he could make a report or give information detrimental to the Transcontinental it gave him the greatest delight.
I want to .show something of the character of the report which the minister received and acted upon. I have only got fragments of the story, but such as they are I gladly give them to him, and I hope at some future date the minister will be able to furnish the committee with the remainder of the data. Away back as early as the 12th of October 1915, Mr. Duff submitted a report to Mr. Gutelius .showing the character of the work which they found under these pedestals. The pedestals, I might explain, are in pairs and are designated No. 1 right, No. 1 left, No. 2 right, No. 2 left, and so on. The bridge sheets show that there should have been 99.16 cuibic yards in No. 4 right, whereas as a matter of fact there were only 57 cubic yards, or a difference of 42.16 cubic yards.- An actual steal of about 40 to 50 per cent. If these contractors and engineers put in only 57 instead of 99 cubic yards in a pedestal supporting a bridge 200 feet high, and then charged for 99 cubic yards and made the public believe they had put in that amount, those men were criminals, and if the minister believed the report he should have had them prosecuted. There is not a man in this House but will agree with me that these men were criminals if, in a bridge of the magnitude I have indicated, over which the traffic of this great transcontinental system was to be carried, they put only 57 cubic yards in the pedestals that required 99 cubic yards.
With respect to No. 13 right, the plan as shown on the bridge sheets calls for 129.49 cubic yards., and the engineers reported that only 89.7 cubic yards were put in, or a difference of 39-79. There again, if these facts are true, every man who had anything to do with the work should have been, prosecuted and sent to the penitentiary for as long a term as possible.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT RAILWAYS-ANNUAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman assert that there was this shortage.''

subtopic: GOVERNMENT RAILWAYS-ANNUAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER.
speechtext:
I say it did not occur. I assert that the statements in the report are absolutely false. If the shortage did
occur, I say that the minister should have prosecuted these men, but I repeat that it did not occur. I shall be able to give some of the facts, and I hope the minister will furnish the Committee with the rest, for he has the whole of them.
There was an individual report on each pedestal. Some of them were shown* to be all right; in others the concrete was claimed to be soft, in others very soft. In some cases it is claimed that a pier that was supposed to have at the base 10 feet, let us say, of solid concrete, had only one foot; in other words, instead of having ten feet of solid concrete from the hard pan up, in order to make a good foundation for the great sturcture, only one foot of concrete was put in, and the remainder was sand. When these facts were investigated further, we found that thgse reports were all false.
I have blue prints here of all the pedestals, nearly 100 of them. There is a plan of each pedestal as it was supposed to have been constructed, and a plan marked over the original showing how the pedestal was constructed according to this report, indicating that there was a shortage of about 30 to 40 per cent, and consequently a steal to that extent.
The contractors for the wprk were as responsible a firm of contractors as ever did business in Canada, Messrs. Powers' & Brewer. These gentlemen began doing business on the Canadian Pacific, they have done business in Nova Scotia, and they are doing business to-day in New Brunswick, and they bear as honorable a name as any contractors in the Dominion. The district engineer was Mr. C. O. Foss who has been connected with railway work in Canada all his lifetime. The divisional engineer was Mr. Balloch. Both of these gentlemen have the highest reputation in their profession. I am not able to say who the resident engineers were. As soon as this report became known, of -course a protest went up. The first protest was made by the contractor, and I want to read to the minister a letter sent by these contractors to the chief engineer of the Transcontinental railway:
March 15 th, 1917.
Gordon Grant, Esq.,
Chief Engineer, Transcontinental Railway Commission,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,
We have received from Mr. Longley copy of Mr. Duff's report on the Little Salmon River pedestals, and the bridge sheets of same showing concrete as returned and also as Mr. Duff claims it was actually constructed.

The charges of over return are absolutely false, and this statement can be easily proven by properly uncovering his most glaring misrepresentations, pedestals 2 R. and L.
We think you should demand that the Government make an independent examination, in justice to all the engineers who were in any way connected with the work, and more particularly ourselves as contractors.
We would be glad to have you advise us if they will do this, and if so, when, so that we may be present and see the pedestals uncovered.
Yours very truly, Powers & Brewer, per H. H. Brewer.
It would take too much time to go through all the correspondence so I will only briefly refer to some of the letters that passed. The contractors demanded that these pedestals, No. 2 right and No. 2 left, be taken, because they were near the bank and it was easy to get at them and they were willing to make these a test of the whole thing. They were willing to try any of them at all, 'but they chose these for the reason I have already given and because they were reported as 'being among the most vicious of all. No. 2 left was the .one concerning which it was said that, after you got to the base of the shaft and came to the pedestal, where there should have been twelve feet of concrete there was only one foot .of concrete. I say again that any firm of contractors, or any engineers that would put in one foot of concrete where there should be twelve, are criminals of the blackest character. It is no wonder that these men protested and demanded that the work should be uncovered, that it might show for itself. I have the correspondence regarding No. 2 pedestal, and I will refer briefly to that correspondence.
First I will call attention to a letter frpm Mr. Duff to Mr. Gordon Grant, stating that they were starting in to repair the substructure, and that if anybody wanted to be present he could attend. Then there is a letter from Mr. Gordon Grant to Messrs. Powers & Brewer which I will read in full:
Ottawa, June Sth, 1916. Messrs. Powers and Brewer,
Contractors, 107 Prince William Street,
St. John, N.B.
Re Little Salmon River.
Dear Sirs,
For your information I enclose herewith copy of letter I have received from W. A. Duff I.C.R. Engineer of Bridges, which speaks for itself. I am sending you this in case you should want to visit the bridge while it is under repair, and you can see for yourself whether or not the representations made by Mr. Duff are correct.
You may notify Mr. Poss, in case he should be sufficiently interested in the matter, to also visit the bridge.

The remainder of the letter merely refers to the fact that the minister had been away and was then busy. Then followed a letter from Messrs. Powers & Brewer to Mr. Gordon Grant, dated I6th June, 1916, acknowledging Mr. 'Grant's letter and proceeding:
We note from Mr. Duff's report of December 29th, 1915, that he intends to entirely rebuild pedestals 10 R. and 11 R., hut the repairs to others will only be to first footing.
If Mr. Duff will advise us when excavation for 10 R. and 11 R. we would like to be present. We would also like to have Mr. Duff uncover the foundations of 2 R. or L. and 15 R. or L. at the same time.	-
No. 15 right was one of the had ones 'according to the first repprt, and 13 right was another very bad one. Then there was a telegram dated 17th July, 1916, from Mr. Brewer to Mr. Duff: [DOT]
Have had no reply to our letter of June 16th to Gordon Grant, copy of which we presume has been forwarded to you. I plan on being at Salmon River Thursday, twentieth, and would like to see pedestal two uncovered. Please wire reply.
H. H. Brewer.
On 18th July, the following answer was sent to Mr. Brewer:
Your wire of seventeenth to hand. Mr. Duff is away at present, will not be back until Thursday.
Regarding the uncovering of pedestals 2 and 15 at Little Salmon River, Mr. Duff is making arrangements to have these pedestals uncovered right away.
He will write and let you know when they are ready for inspection.
This was followed by a letter from Messrs. Power & Brewer to Mr. Gordpn Grant, dated 19th June:
Yours of 16th instant enclosing copy of Mr. Duff's letter of June 13th received.
Would it not be possible for you to arrange with Mr. Duff to have the excavating around pedestals No. 2 done at once?
Then there is the following letter from Mr. Duff to Messrs. Powers & Brewer:
Moncton, N.B., August 11th, 1916. Messrs. Powers and Brewer,
Contractors,
107 Prince William Street,
St. John, N.B.
Little Salmon River Viaduct.
Gentlemen:
Referring to your letter of June 19th to Mr. Gordon Grant and my letter to Mr. H. H. Brewer of the 11th July.
We have now excavated to the bottom of foundation of pedestal 2 R, and I will be obliged if you will make arrangements to visit the site of the bridge for the purpose of inspecting this at an early date, as it will not do for us to leave the foundation uncovered very long.
I am sorry that we have been unable to uncover pedestal No. 15 R or L. as yet on

account of water conditions. Will you please advise me when you will visit the site of the bridge, as I would like to be there at the same time if possible.
Yours truly,

This, it will 'be seen, is a notification that they have excavated to the bottom of pedestal No. 2 right. If they had done so, there could not be very much difficulty in finding out who was right and who was wrong. Mr. Brewer sends back a letter dated 15th August, 1916, addressed to 'Mr. Duff:
Yours of 11th instant received. We have had No. 2 pedestal examined by Mr. M. J. Powers of Grand Falls, and he advises us that in his opinion your excavation does not reach the bottom of the pedestal but only to a set of walling timbers inside the sheet piling.
He advises that it would not be of any use for me to go up until he is satisfied that the excavation has been carried to bottom of footing course. Will you please have this done, and X would then be pleased to meet you there.
Then, on August 22, there is another letter to Mr. Duff from Messrs. Powers & Brewer, as follows:
Please advise if you are arranging for further excavation of No. 2 pedestal as asked for in our letter of 15th instant.
We are anxious to have the letter cleared up as soon as possible.
Mr. Duff answers on 26th August:
We are arranging for further excavation of pedestal No. 2 and will advise you as soon as I get definite information with regard to same.
It will be noted that three weeks before this they had reported to the engineer that they had uncovered No. 2 pedestal. The contractor sent a man there who saw that they had not uncovered it at all. And on the 26th August they say:	"We are arranging for further excavation," and " will advise you." And they did. On the 22nd September they wrote again:
Referring to your letter of the 22 nd of August, and mine of the 26th of August.
We have excavated as far down as pedestal No. 2 as it is safe for us to do-
They did not go to the bottom, but the^ excavated as far as it was safe to do.
.-and we have drilled an inch and a half hole through the footing course, and find it to be eight feet thick.
Will you please advise me if you wish to examine this pedestal any further, as we wish to fill in the excavation within a short time?
Then, to follow the history of that one transaction, Mr. Duff did not hesitate to report to the minister and to the country that responsible engineers and contractors had built a pedestal one foot thick when it should have been 11 or 12 feet thick under
a bridge of the magnitude of that which I have described, or to say that he had dug down and uncovered one side of every pedestal in the whole bridge. If you want confirmation of that, you will find it in the report in which they say they dug down one side to the bottom, and assuming that this pedestal was square they figured out the contents. Here is a case where they reported one foot of concrete. But the contractor said: "You are wrong." He even said worse than that. They were sent back and they dug again, and they went down a little way and they said: "We were to the bottom." The contractor sent a man down to look at it, and he said: "You are not at the bottom." They said: "We will dig a little further," and they went on and dug eight feet, and still they did not go to the bottom. Then they would not dig any more, and they tried to drill, but they admitted that they never got to the bottom. They admit eight feet of solid concrete in their report instead of only one foot. I would like to know what the minister has to say of engineers who are making reports of that class, and thereby attempting to blast the reputation of honourable men who are trying to earn an honest living. I have given the facts regarding this No. 2 pedestal. They said that it was not necessary to go to the bottom to show that it was proper work, but Mr. C. O. Foss, the district engineer, followed these men to the very end. The contractors did not propose to be put in a false light by these men if they could help it. However, I do not believe that it was Mr. Duff; I believe the real man behind him was Mr. Gutelius. They reached the point, in the month of October, I think, when Duff had to say that he would not dig any further. Finally he named a day when he would be present to go over the work with Messrs. Powers and Brewer. He said that it would be some day next week. Mr. Brewer, who was the man having charge of the work, remained in St. John a whole week, but never was called upon, and finally was notified by Duff that he had to go away and could not meet him, but that he would send one of his assistants. Duff did not dare to go on the work with Powers and Brewer, and therefore sent his subordinate. The subordinate went there.
Do the papers give the name of the subordinate?

Yes, Mr. Leightner,
representing Duff, and the representatives of the contracting firm appeared on the ground. I have in my possession, and I

want to read, a letter addressed by C. O. Foss, district engineer, to Gordon Grant, dated the 7th November, 1916, which purports to give the result of that interview. If this be true, and the minister will know whether it is or not, it reveals a condition of affairs for which the minister ought to make a public apology to these contractors and to the engineers connected with the matter. It is as follows:
Nov. 7th, 1916.
Gordon Grant, Esq.,
Chief Engineer, N.T.R.
Little Salmon River Viaduct.
Dear Sir:-
Since your communication of the 8th of June I have tried, in conjunction with Messrs. Powers and Brewer, to get something definite from Mr. Duff either confirming or disproving his charges of last year, As you know we asked to have the foundations of pedestals Nos. 2 and 15 uncovered as two of the most glaring examples he had1 reported of work that was not done. On August 11th he wrote me that he had excavated down to the bottom of foundation of pedestal No. 2R and notified me that if I wanted to inspect it I must do so at an early date as he would not leave the excavation open very long.
On the same date he wrote Powers and Brewer to the same effect and added in tihe letter to them that he had not been able to excavate down to the bottom of the foundation of No. 15 owing to water conditions. This was not surprising to us as we knew that it would be absolutely impossible to excavate to the bottom of either of these pedestals without the use of a powerful pump, though from his report of last year he apparently had no trouble from water conditions then. On the day we received the letters from Duff, Mr. Powers' brother, who lives at Grand Falls and was watching the work, reported that they had not reached the bottom of No. 2R, and Mr. Brewer so notified Mr. Duff. Some time later, on September 22nd, he wrote Brewer that they had excavated as far down on pedestal No. 2R as it was safe for them to do and had drilled an inch and a half hole through the footing course and found it 8 feet thick.
Following this there was considerable more correspondence which culminated in an agreement by Mr. Brewer to meet Mr. Duff on the site upon the receipt of a wire; finally Duff wrote and wired that his assistant Mr. Leightner would meet him or his representative on Tuesday, October 31st, and as Mr. Brewer had already made an engagement in Montreal for that date he had to send his accountant and Powers whom I have mentioned before. As a result of that meeting we have the following admissions.
This is the point. I am reading now from a statement by Mr. Foss to the chief engineer, and the minister will know whether that statement is correct or not.
In the case of No. 2R as I have already stated he admits that he has drilled through a footing 8 feet thick instead of one foot as reported last year. In the case of No. 10R they removed it altogether and admit that it was 13-6 deep, being nearly 2 feet more than they 
found last year. No. 150R they admit is 14-7 to bottom, which is nearly 5 feet more than they found last year. No. 4R they found nearly 5 feet more than last year, and at No. 13R about 4 feet more. They state that Mr. Leightner is prepared to admit that the report of last year is not correct. Of course this is quite superfluous as the figures given prove that. I am quite satisfied that if they will send another investigating party there who is anxious to get the truth they will find the balance which they claim is still lacking as shown by our bridge sheets. Mr. Brewer and self intend to interview Mr. Brown soon with a view to learning his attitude with regard to the matter of last year's charges in the light of the information obtained this summer. If you put the figures I have given you on your sheets you will see at a glance how the matter stands under their present , claim. I trust you will bring the matter to the attention of the minister in order that he may understand that by their own present findings we are relieved of the great part of the charges made last year.	.
All the answer there is to that is a simple acknowledgement by Mr. Grant stating that he had forwarded a copy of the letter to the minister, and as it was forwarded to the minister, no doubt he caused an investigation to be made, and he will be able to tell us whether the admission of Mr. Leightner is correct or not. I am sorry that my voice is in such a condition that I will not be able to follow this up very much further. I do not intend to weary the committee by going into the details at any greater extent. I have shown the minister two things. First, his engineers reported to him that they had made an actual investigation of every one of those pedestals, when they did not. There is no getting away from that. These men never measured those pedestals, and I doubt very much if they ever measured any single pedestal out of the whole hundred. That is a pretty strong statement. In the first place, there could not be very many of them measured without very extensive pumping arrangements, because that is in a great valley, and when those pedestals were put down, they had to pump water continuously, and the cost was much more excessive than they imagined it would be, on account of the difficulty in keeping the water out of the cofferdam. They never could have measured down to the bottom of any of them, and we have now the admission of four or five of these people that what they did make was all wrong, in Nos. 2, 4, 10 and 13; because, in this case, they dug down and found they were all wrong. They blasted out concrete which was as solid as anything could possibly be in this world, unless if were steel.
I will bring samples and show them to the minister. I have a sample of rock blasted out of one of the pedestals, where the con-

Crete was so solid and firm that the blasting broke the rock, instead of breaking the concrete, and I think the minister received samples of the same kind, where they blew these pedestals out with dynamite, in order to put in new ones. I do not know how many men they have employed there, but they must have squandered at least $00,000 or $70,000 in carrying on this unnecessary work, and for what purpose I cannot imagine. I know it was used as a political machine. I know that scores of men were employed upon it, for the purpose of getting their votes at the next provincial election, and they did not get the votes, if that is any satisfaction to the minister.
I know thousands of dollars	were
thrown into the pockets of Mr. White, who ran a general store at Grand Falls, and who was then representing the county in the local legislature, but he is not representing it now. I know it was the greatest piece of political * jugglery that has taken place in New Brunswick in my day. There was probably $50,000 or $60,000 of public money absolutely wasted in tearing out concrete piers, which would have been there a thousand years hence, if left alone, and they replaced them with concrete piers, no better than the former ones.
What year was this done?

Last year, when the provincial elections were coming on, and I suppose they expected a Dominion election as well.' This is one of the greatest scandals, considering the amount of money involved, that has ever taken place in that country. It is a by-word among the people for miles and miles around. I have letters, which I suppose I should not refer to, from engineers on the American side of the boundary line, who heard about this business and came over, not one but many, to see what kind of butchery the Government was carrying on. I have received correspondence from these engineers stating their opinions about it. And yet the minister squandered all this money, and has nothing to show for it, excepting, I suppose, he will say he knows now what the bottoms are. The bottoms were' there all right, but the $60,000 or $70,000 is gone. We can forgive him if he will publicly apologize to the men who have been slandered by his general manager and the officials of his department. That- will atone to some extent for the wrong done by this piece of political jobbery.

The hon. gentleman from Carleton told me this afternoon that he intended to bring this matter before the committee. I told him that I had not all the papers here, and I wante4 him to postpone it, but he said he would rather not. In reference to his charges against Mr. Gutelius he is absolutely unfair, because what first brought it to the general manager's notice was the resident engineer, Mr. R. A. Black, reporting to the superintendent, Mr. H. B. Fleming, on an examination made by him of the substructure of the Salmon river viaduct on the National Transcontinental east of Grand Falls station, and finds there is a rise of ten inches in the first span going into the bridge. This is due to a settlement of the abutment and the girders should be jacked up to place, and the bridge seat raised to the proper level either with concrete or capstones, also that many of the pedestals are in a bad and dangerous shape, on account of defective concrete having been used, etc.
I have a short report of what was done, as follows:
During the past summer repairs to the substructure of this bridge were carried out under the supervision of Mr. James Finley, and twenty pedestals in all were repaired, these being 3R, 3L, 4R, 4>L, 5R, 5L, 6L, 7R, 7L, 8R, SL, 9R, 9L, 10R, 10D, HR, 12R, 15D, 19L and 25L. The details of the repairs which were done to these pedestals are given in report dated the 10th of November, from Mr. Finley to me, covering the work done during the past summer, copy of which report I attach hereto.
You will note in Mr. Finley's report that he recommends that the following pedestals should be repaired next year:-11L, 13L, 14L, 28R, 28L, 34L, 37L, 39L and 43R.
During the present summer the actual size of the following six pedestals were determined : -2R, 4R, 2L, 10R, 13R and 15R. Pedestals 2R, 4R, 4D and 13R were measured in the presence of Messrs. Powers and Tilley of the firm of Powers and Brewer, Finley, Oulton, Bridge and Building Master Turner and Assistant Engineer G. C. Leightner. It was necessary to entirely remove pedestal 10R, and pedestal 15R was excavated to the bottom of the foundation under Mr. Finley and the depth of the foundation thus determined. The measurements of these pedestals show that there is one hundred and forty-two yards less concrete in them than is Shown on original bridge sheets.
I would like to call your attention particularly to the quality of the concrete taken out of the pedestals which were repaired this year, as shown in Mr. Finley's report.
The repairs which were undertaken this year under the supervision of Mr. Finley bear out fully the information given in my report of December 28, 1915, to you, as to the quality of the concrete and the necessity for making the repairs. When the concrete was taken out of the pedestals, the quality of same was found, if anything, to be worse than indicated in my report to you and some idea of the quality of the original concrete put in these pedestals may be obtained from looking at photographs

attached to Mr. Finley's report of pedestals HR and 12R.
On October 1 sent Mr. G. C. Leightner, Assistant Engineer, to this bridge to meet Messrs. Joe Powers and Tilley of the firm of Powers and Brewer, and he examined the foundation of pedestals 2R, 4R, 4L and 13'R in their presence and also in the presence of Messrs. Finley, Oulton and Bridge and Building Master Turner. Mr. Lightner reported to me in connection with pedestal 2R as follows:
"A rod was thrust into the hole which Mr. Finley had bored through the footing and depth measured as a little over eight feet. A rod was then driven some three feet further and then pulled out and the last three feet of the rod were found to be covered with mud. Mr. Tilley was satisfied to accept the thickness of eight feet which Mr. Finley had reported, but Mr. Powers, however, was still sceptical and asked to have another hole drilled in the footing so that he could watch the drilling. Mr. Finley offered to do this for him if he, Mr. Powers, would pay the expense of drilling providing Mr. Finley's finding of eight feet was confirmed. This offer was not accepted. Mr. Powers gave his ground for belief in this pedestal extending deeper, that the man who inspected the work on this pedestal was on his first job of inspection and, he said, would therefore be most careful to have the work done in accordance with the plans."
In connection with pedestal 4R, Mr. Lightner reports:
"Giving them-the contractors-the benefit of every doubt, we concluded the measurement to be 13{ 11" from the top of the pedestal to the pedestal to the top of the bottom footing and 16' 7" from the top of the pedestal to the bottom of the bottom footing. The bridge sheet shows these two dimensions as 13.7' and 17.7', or 1.1' deeper than we found."
With regard to pedestal 4L, he reports:
"The total depth is 2' 4" less than shown on the bridge sheet."
With regard to pedestal 13R, Mr, Lightner reports the total height to be 2' 6" less than shown on the bridge sheet.
Mr. Leightner's report says:	"Got very
little satisfaction from either Mr. Powers or Mr. Tilley as to the quality of the concrete which had been removed. They both se<?med to think that the concrete when first put in, although the gravel might not have been as good as possible, was of good quality, and that their workmanship had been as good as ordinary, and that the present condition of the pedestals was due to deterioration which might happen to concrete any place.	They cited several
examples of work in Nova Scotia, which I understood they had built and were now having to rebuild. As to the quality of the gravel which was used, Mr. Powers was inclined to blame the engineers in charge; that is, he stated that the engineers in charge inspected and passed all material used, and if unsatisfactory got into the work, it was not the contractors' fault.
My opinion from the appearance of the broken concrete which had been removed from the pedestals _ is that in general the concrete was poorly mixed, not properly tamped in the forms, contained insufficient cement and somewhat dirty aggregate and altogether too large a quantity of plums, some of them not judicially placed.''
I have some photographs here, and I leave it to any man who examines them to

say whether the concrete is good. Several of the photographs show that the concrete could be picked out without blasting or anything of that kind. Some portions of the cement are good, but others are not. In a bridge of that size, bad concrete is apt to crumble out; the work can hardly he said to be proper if there is a had mixture of cement. If Mr. Powers, wants to be prosecuted in the matter, I think that we can put up a case that will hang him.
You had better go to work and do it, then.
I shall be very glad to get a full report and present it later.

On a previous occasion the attention of the minister was directed to the so-called embargo which was put upon the shipment of grain from the prairie west during last fall and winter. I offer no apology for mentioning the matter again and asking the minister whether there is, under the authority with which he is vested, any remedy for that condition; because when a shipment of grain is refused, a serious loss is suffered by the owner who desires to ship it.
Where was the embargo placed?

On all lines in Alberta from the Canadian Pacific Railway main line north as far as the Saskatchewan river. Notices were issued from time to time by the railway companies that they would not take grain for shipment to Port William or to Minneapolis-though they would take grain for shipment to the interior elevators. There is no doubt that tlie railway companies did this under the authority of the Railway Commission. I want to know, on behalf of the people interested, if there is any authority higher than the Railway Commission. Have the people of western Canada any remedy in this matter, which, affecting, as it does, the shipment of their produce, is to them a matter, if not of actual, at any rate of profitable, existence?

This is the first time that the putting on of an embargo by the railways has been drawn to my attention.
I will inquire into the matter. I will try to get the information for my hon. friend from the Railway Commission.
My hon. friend surely remembers our discussing the matter in the House on a previous occasion.
When?
On the occasion, I think, of the Budget debate.
I was not present then.

I know that there was an exchange between my hon. friend and myself on that subject on a previous occasion during this session. However, let it be noted that this is a matter in which the people are deeply interested. They want to know if the railway companies are being supported in their refusal to act as common carriers and to take freight to such destination as is indicated by the shipper. My information is that in a certain case a man had 17,000 bushels of threshed oats lying in his field contiguous to the Canadian Pacific main line a little east of Calgary, and the shipment of that grain to Fort William or Minneapolis was refused him by the railway company. That was one instance. It is a general case I desire to make my statement on, and I desire to get the best attention in regard to it.
Mr. COCHEANE.:	I will get the information.

The minister said a few
minutes ago that the Government had never refused to accept shipments over the Transcontinental. These three railroad systems in the Prairie West are naturally the feeders to the Transcontinental; it is over those lines or some of them, at any Tate, that the business must come that the Transcontinental shall handle, and when those railway companies refuse to take grain for shipment to Winnipeg or Fort William, of course, that business is not there for the Transcontinental to handle. If the minister, will pardon me for saying so, it seems a strange administration of a great railway [DOT]system in the hands of the Government of our country, when such a condition can exist without the knowledge of the head of that administration.
In regard to the removal of rails on the Grand Trunk Pacific west of Edmonton, in iwha't manner are the interests of the coal mines on either side of Jasper and Brule lakes being protected?

The matter of the three transcontinental railways west of Winnipeg bringing goods to the Transcontinental for shipment does not require very much explanation, because two of them run Tight through to the Atlantic, and we have to depend on what the Grand Trunk Pacific brings to the Transcontinental.
So far as the removal of rails is concerned, my engineer returned on Saturday, on which day I unfortunately had to be away, I hope to-morrow to be able to ask my hon. friend
to change his question into an order for return, and I will endeavour to lay on the Table to-morrow full particulars in reference to that matter.

In regard to the lifting
of Tails on the Transcontinental between Winnipeg and Quebec, the House is entitled to a definite statement as to what rails have been lifted and as to how far the lifting of those rails might effect the successful operation of the railway.

The first 300 miles of
rails have been lifted and are now either gone overseas or waiting for shipment. I will lay on the Table a plan showing where
those rails have been lifted.
How many tons of those rails are now piled on the dock at Three Eivers?
I do not know. I will try to find out.

Two weeks ago the
minister stated in answer to a question of mine that the Government's policy in regard to the railway situation in Canada .would be announced very shortly. Will the policy of the Government regarding the railway situation in Canada, consequent on the two reports of the Eoyal Commissioners, be announced within the next few days?

The Government is
not ready yet to make its announcement, and I cannot say just when it will be.

That answer is as indefinite as Government answers to questions of .that kind usually are. I do not know that I can blame the minister any more than any of his predecessors in regard to such answers, because that is the kind that is usually given. The railway situation in Canada, notwithstanding the great war that is going on, is the most serious proposition that Canada has to face. The war is undoubtedly a serious matter, but the present railway situation in Canada will, in the near future, tax the ability and energy of the best men that Canada can produce. The Government have appointed a Eoyal Commission consisting of three notable men of experience in railway matters, and those men have agreed that the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific are bankrupt, and that if the Grand Trunk Eailway Company is compelled to carry out its obligation entered into with the Government in regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental, the Grand Trunk



Railway Company will also become bankrupt. That being the situation, the Government should, in the interest of the country, immediately announce a policy on this very momentous and important question. I presume that the Government will do in this matter what it has hitherto done in regard to other matters of a similar kind, and what probably other governments have done in matters of equal importance, and that is, leave the question until the dying days of the session, and then bring in the most important legislation which will be before Parliament during this session, to be disposed of in four or five of the closing days of Parliament. I, for one, wish to protest most energetically against such a situatioh.' No further money should be voted in reference to the railway management in this country until the Government shall have announced its railway policy, because the matter is too important. I have no criticism to make against the Minister of Railways and Canals-, so far as my knowledge *of the situation is concerned, he is as good *a Minister of Railways as we have ever -had, and perhaps that is not damning him with very great praise. But the existing railway situation in Canada is too important to be trifled with or to be postponed until the closing days of the session, and I wish to give the minister warning now that he will hear from me about this matter in other sessions in this committee until we have an announcement of what policy the Government purpose pursuing in regard to this very serious and important situation.

I agree with my hin. friend that the railway situation is very serious, and it deserves and will receive the consideration of the Government; but to say that it is the greatest problem before the Government is not true; the war is the greatest problem, and that we will attend to first. The Bill introduced to-day is the most important legislation ever introduced in this country, and until that is disposed of we cannot expect to- deal with much more legislation.
Will an opportunity be given, when the minister's estimates are up again, to discuss the information he is to lay on the Table to-morrow?
Oh, yes.

Wh-at amounts were spent last year for betterments on that section of

the Intercolonial between Point Tupper and Sydney?
I made a note of the hon. gentleman's remarks before dinner and wired to Moncton for the information. As soon as I receive it I shall be glad -to communicate it.
Is the minister proceeding with the construction of a viaduct at Trenton, in the county of Pictou, to avoid the railroad tracks in connection with the steel company?
I think there is an item in the Estimates for that. I will let my hon. friend know later on.
What is the situation with regard -to t'he coal supply for the Intercolonial? Have arrangements been made for the coming year, and contracts been let?

We have bought all the coal we need for the Intercolonial and the eastern part of the Transcontinental, except about 75,000 tons. At the head of the lakes we have about that amount for the Transcontinental in the West.
Where was this coal purchased?
Some from American coal companies, and some front Montreal. We have also two boats carrying coal from Sydney to Levis, to supply that port and points down to Riviere du Loup.
What coal companies are supplying this coal for the Transcontinental and the Intercolonial?
I cannot give that information to-night, but I will get it for my hon. friend.
Has the question of the Acadia Company been settled yet?
For 25,000 tons.

25,000 tons have been ordered at $4.25?
Yes.

been accepted?
Yes.

I have not the figures, but will get them for my hon. friend.
The minister cannot expect to get his Estimates through unless he supplies us with the usual information; it is not the practice of Parliament.
If the hon. gentleman will tell me what information he wants, I shall be glad to get it for him. It would take a Philadelphia lawyer to carry all this information in one's head.

The minister cannot assume that attitude with me; it may do with some people, but not with me. Every other minister, when his estimates are up, is prepared to give the Committee this ordinary information.

I told my hon. friend I would get the information for him as soon as possible.

The Minister of Marine and Fisheries, when his estimates were before the House two or three days ago, did not adopt the attitude of my hon. friend, but had his officials here and was ready and anxious to give all the information that was asked for; there was no delay. The minister knows that my questions are reasonable.
Carried.

speechtext:
I was pointing out that it is the practice with ministers at the head of great spending departments such as this, to come prepared with in* formation on most ordinary questions that are likely to crop up. In regard to the
im
questions asked by myself and by my colleagues, the minister has given us no information at all.

We are not on the
item of coal, anyway.
There is no item for coal.
It comes under operating expenses, and that is not under discussion now.

I have asked the
minister whether he proposes to construct' the viaduct at Trenton in the county of Pictou, and if so, is it to be done by contract or day labour? I should also like a full statement of what coal he has purchased for the Intercolonial, from whom, and at what price. If the minister says he will give me that information at an early date I have no more to say, except that he should be prepared to furnish the committee with information of this kind when his Estimates are up.

I was somewhat disappointed at being unable to get the information I asked for with regard to the expenditure for betterments on the Intercolonial. The item before the committee is for construction and betterments on the Canadian Government railways, $6,500,000. It is well known that for the past two or three years the Department of Railways and Canals has been spending a very considerable amount of money on the Intercolonial railway between Point Tupper and Sydney for straightening curves, reducing grades, putting in concrete culverts and approaches. I congratulate the minister on these expenditures, which are very important to that section of the road, but I am bound to say with all deference that I did hope to be able to get the information I asked for this evening. I am not finding fault with the minister, but inasmuch as there is a great deal of information pertaining to this particular item to which the committee is entitled, I should be glad if the minister would allow the item to stand for the present.

I was to inquire further of the minister regarding the report of the Royal Commission on the railway situation. I think the House should have this information at a very learly date. The report of Sir Henry Drayton and Mr. Acworth states that the Grand Trunk Railway Company claim to be, and in the opinion of both these gentlemen are. re-

lieved from legal liability in connection with the operation of the Transcontinental portion of the system under the terms of the agreement. Has the minister had any opinion from the Department of Justice, or, if not, will he secure an opinion from that department,, to inform the House whether or not this company is relieved from legal obligation to operate the portion of the railway built by the Government from Winnipeg to Moncton? For, if they are legally relieved from this obligation, it can only be by reason of the fact that the contract entered into between the Government and the Grand Trunk Company has been violated by the Government; no violation of that contract by the Grand Trunk Railway Company or by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, could relieve the Grand Trunk Company from this liability. This House and the country ought to know whether the company has been relieved from its legal obligation. This is an exceedingly serious matter, far too serious to be passed over without full information and thorough investigation.

I fully sympathize with what has been brought to the attention of the minister by the hon. member for Welland. This and other large questions will have to be dealt with when the matter comes before the House. But there are some matters of a local character relating to my own constituency, which I desire to call to the attention of the minister. These may appear small matters, but this is the only railway operated in the part of the country from which I come, and the minister is the one representative of the owners of that railway before whom we can bring any difficulties or grievances, and so we must bring to his attention small matters as well as great ones. By correspondence, I have already brought to the notice of the minister the fact that there is a good deal of faultfinding in the county of Cape Breton and the county of Victoria, by reason of the fact that the people are refused proper railway crossings. It was in 1887, I think, that the right-of-way for this railway in the island of Cape Breton was obtained. That is a

good many years ago, and at that time the farming population of Cape Breton, and the products of the farms there were not as important as they are to-day, nor was there such a call for farming as there is at present. In those days, it was quite common to have a farm of two or three hundred acres, and for each farm there would be one crossing. But in many cases it has happened that one or two sons have taken fifty or a hundred acres of the old farm and have started farming on their own account. Yet the Department of Railways, as I understand it, refuses to give more crossings. It is not very much encouragement for a young man to remain on the land and carry on' the agricultural' production that we consider to-day so very necessary to find that he is refused a farm crossing, in fact that may make the difference between the young man starting a farm or not starting it. I have in mind a case where the railway not only cuts a young man's farm in two, tout runs between him and the post road, and so in order to reach the Toad he must go over to his father's farm and get out by way of the old crossing. There should be more sympathy between the railway management and the farmers in these matters. I have understood that the reason crossings were not granted was that the railway officials did not want to establish a precedent. But there should be no feeling of that kind on their part. To accommodate the farmers in these matters means to develop the country. Even if a farm crossing should cost $100-and few of these crossings, I think, would cost more-the expenditure would be a good one and one with which, I am sure, the members of this House would not find fault. I trust that a more generous policy in this matter will ibe adopted by the department and that the officers on the line, the track-masters and superintendents, will not regard the farmer who asks for a crossing as a man who. is trying to make trouble. It is a matter of general complaint against the bon. minister's officers that they are not in sympathy with those in whose way difficulties are placed, or to whom damage is caused by the railway. So long as the Government runs this road it must expect the same kind of trouble that other railways have., It is more difficult to get at a Government-owned railway by means of the courts, and for that very reason it should be made more easy to approach the officials of the department and get matters of this kind settled.
JUNE 11, m7
At our end of the line, at Sydney, North Sydney and Sydney Mines, there is great reason to complain because of the irregularity of the trains.' This irregularity has continued for nine months or a year past. Trains due at nine o'clock in the morning frequently do not arrive until four o'clock in the afternoon, though they oome only from Halifax, a distance of 250 miles. Some say that the irregularity of the trains is due to bad coal, some that it is due to bad engines, while others say that the track is to blame. Wherever the difficulty lies, at least it will be easy for the minister to find out the facts as to the irregularity we complain about, if any record is kept of the time when the trains leave Halifax and when they arrive at Sydney. Several letters have been sent to me and business people, and those who Havel over this road have asked me to bring this matter to the attention of the minister and see if something can be done for a betterment in this regard.
I would like to also mention to the minister that between our town and Sydney we had very poor accommodation last year. We have a local service when there is ice in the harbour. In the summer we have no local service and there is no necessity for it. We have only one local train a day between Florence, Sydney Mines, North Sydney and Sydney. Last year the first train we could get from North Sydney to Sydney was at two o'clock in the afternoon. To do business, or to attend court in Sydney, we must be there at ten in the morning. The minister will tell me that we should get there on the express in the morning and the fast train coming in at night. But the train is often late and you can never tell when it is coming in. If you have any important business in Sydney you have to leave the night before on the evening express so that you may be sure of being there. In other years we had the train leaving at nine in the morning and that took people from Florence, Sydney Mines and North Sydney to Sydney. But this year instead of the nine o'clock train, we have to depend on the incoming express which, nine times out of ten, is late and there is a feeling on the part pf the business people that it cannot be depended upon. I hope that the minister will instruct his officers to have a proper local service next winter because we cannot toe left' to depend upon the service we had last year.

In reference to my
hon. friend's complaint abput crossings, we
have endeavoured to do as other railways do, but as we propose putting the Government railways under the Railway Commission, these matters will be settled by them if they are not being attended to as it is thought they should be by the minister. With reference to the local train, I have made a note of it and we will discuss it with our officers before winter comes and see what can be done.

I am glad to hear the
minister say that the trunk lines of the Government railways are going to 'be put under the Railway Commission. Is it the intention to have provincially chartered branch lines also placed under the Railway Commission? Will the Railway Commission give 'a through Tate on freight arising on a branch line constructed under a provincial charter a number of years ago and connecting with the trunk line?
I would like to call the minister's attention to the condition of the Caraquet railway, an enterprise that is very much retarded because of the lack of equipment and proper roadbed. It is proposed in some cases to increase the rate 50 per cent in order to make up the earnings. Lack of equipment, especially of facilities for dealing with snowstorms during the winter, is one of the difficulties with which the road has to contend. I hope, however, now that the trunk line of the Government railways is to he under the Railway Commission, that it will have some control over the branch lines that are feeders to the trunk line. It is a matter of great importance to the communities that are served by these branch lines that have been constructed under provincial charters. I would ask the minister to make a note of this, and see what can be done at the earliest' opportunity. I would urge the minister, in the public interest, to make an effort to come to some terms with the bondholders of the Caraquet railway, and take over the management of . that piece of road. The road has good earning power but the rails are light, the roadbed is in a bad condition, and during the stormy portion of the season they can do nothing but battle with the storm. Perishable freight is left where it arises, and a great loss occurs to the commercial interests of that part of the country. We talk about production, we are urging production, but how can production be overtaken if there are no facilities for moving the products to the market? This is a portion of the country that has not the

transportation facilities that it requires for the carriage of its products.
I would also like to ask the minister if any progress is being made with regard to the construction of a bridge from Chelmsford to Millertown? The minister said that he would take the matter up with the local Government, and that he hoped that the local Government would make some move in that direction. He intimated that the Railway Department could perhaps 'find1 the iron work of the bridge. It is the imperative duty of the Government to provide communication from the Chelmsford side of the river. The minister took the rails up for 26 miles along that part of the river, the residents of that section have no railway facilities whatever, and they have no means of crossing the river to the railway that is operated on the other side. I believed the minister was in earnest when he told us that arrangements would be made with the local Government with a view to having that bridge constructed. The survey was made, and I have no doubt the report of the survey is in the department. I am not prepared to say that it was finally made, but I know that some location was made in view of the possibility of the bridge being constructed either by the Federal or the Provincial Government. The minister will recall that a few years ago the?e was a contract entered into for the construction of a Y at Derby Junction. For some reason, which I have never been able to understand, the contract was cancelled, and the Y was not constructed. When representatives of my town called upon the manager, he said that if it was found to be unsatisfactory he would endeavour to have [DOT] the Y constructed. The matter has remained in that position. The local train runs from Loggieville to Derby Junction and stops there, and it cannot turn because there is no "Y" there, and it must back into Chatham. I should like to know why the "Y" was not constructed at Derby Junction. I hope the minister will take that into consideration.

It is impossible to bring these branch lines, constructed under provincial charter, under the Railray Board, unless they are declared to be works for' the general advantage of Canada. It would be strong handed work for the Government to place them under the Railway Board. The "Y" cannot be proceeded with, because we cannot get rails.
That is a good reason.

WTe have taken up a good many branches, in order to procure rails. We have succeeded in placing a contract for 10,000 tons of rails with the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. I think the hon. gentleman is mistaken in reference to that bridge. I do not think I made the promise he refers to. The promise may have been made in my absence by someone else.
I am glad the hon. gentleman has given the reason why the "Y" was not constructed, and I am pleased to have his promise that when the rails are available it will be constructed.
I did not make the promise.
Better make it at once.
I do not make promises

On whose report or advice was the track removed from the main line of railway at the wharf at Saokville?
The track was taken up because we wanted the rails. We do not propose to abandon it; we shall replace it as soon as we can get rails.

In discussing the removal of rails from the Transcontinental the other day, the minister intimated that only a certain kind of rail would serve the purpose for which rails were required on the other side. The piece of track to which I refer is not more than half a mile long. Some years ago a large wharf was built at Sackville at a cost of about $40,000, and, as it was not connected with the main line of railway, it could not be used. Subsequently the Government, at considerable expense, repaired an old wharf to which there was access by rail. For two years, during the construction of the car ferry terminals at Cape Tormentine, it has (been impossible to use the pier at Cape Tormentine for the shipment of lumber and other commodities, and the Sackville wharf has been used for that purpose. Last March the rails connecting with the wharf were taken up, and business men who had 'built warehouses on the wharf and stored in them large quantities of fertilizer and other goods were subjected to great loss and inconvenience. It is unfortunate that the only means of shipping in that section of the country should have been suddenly taken away. I agree that when rails are required we should give as many as we can. But I understood from the discussion the other day that in the case of the removal of rails in other localities, care was taken that there should be uo serious interference with business arrangements and that proper accommodation should be given in some other way. In this case it is not possible to make other satisfactory arrangements under which the business people of the locality affected may use the wharf. I think, therefore, that the minister was ill-

advised in taking up that short piece of track, thereby occasioning great loss to the shippers and to the people generally of that locality.

Some six years ago the Department of Railways decided to build two subways at St. Fabien, in the county of Rimouski, one at the east and one at the west end of the station. Although the subway proposed to be built at the east end of the station was the one most necessary, the one at the west was built, while the construction of the other was postponed. The siding at the station completely blocks the public crossing, and people travelling to the village have often been detained in winter from thirty to forty-five minutes being unable to cross the track. These delays occasion great annoyance and inconvenience. I understand that for many years provision had been made in the Estimates for completing the construction of both subways, but up to the present time the one at the east has not been built. I would ask the Minister of Railways to look into this matter and to do the best he can to make this improvement as soon as possible. In view of the nature of the crossings and the need for improved facilities, this subway is one of the most urgently required improvements on the Intercolonial railway. Upon approaching the track, the farmers have to climb a heavy hill. At the top the ground is level for a distance of about twenty-five or thirty feet, and sometimes ten or fifteen teams collect on that small piece of ground. There is a downhill slope on the other side of the track, and the whole crossing is very dangerous. If the minister will examine the plans and reports that have been made on the subject, he will realize the truth of what I am saying and appreciate the benefit that the construction of this improvement would be to the public in that locality.

I shall be very glad to , 'have the matter looked into, and if the situation is as the hon. member says it is, there is no question that there ought to be a crossing at that point, andi we will see what can be done.

This item in the
Estimates this year is in a peculiar situation. There does not appear to 'be any vote upon income for the Intercolonial, and the only item which relates to the Canadian Government railways is contained in this one on page 52 of the Estimates:
Construction and betterments, Dartmouth to Deans, branch line, and to provide car ferry- construction terminals, etc.

I would gather from what the minister said with regard to construction and betterments that he included a large expenditure for bridges and roadbed on the Prince Edward Island railway. Do I understand that notwithstanding the fact that this is war time, the minister purposes making this very large capital expenditure in Prince Edward Island for the purpose of changing the gauge of the railway?
No.

What then is the
minister intending to do with all this money?

I read out what we
were doing.

It is on account of
what the minister stated in a general way -so many hundred thousand dollars for roadbed and! so many for bridges-that I asked the question. Those items I would have thought would naturally have come out of income and not be charged to capital unless they involved a change of gauge.
There is only $900 for bridges in Prince Edward Island.
Am I to understand that the changing of the gauge of the Prince Edward Island railway for the purpose of utilising the car ferry is not to be made now ?

I impressed upon
the minister twice this session the necessity of securing an increased quantity of rolling-stock for the purpose of ensuring the transportation of coal. The coal situation in Canada is very serious. By reason of the fact that the vessels engaged in the transportation of coal from Nova Scotia to the St. Lawrence river having been commandeered, and that at the present moment it is problematical whether arrangements can be made for transporting the coal at Nova Scotia ports, the question is very grave as to whether the people of Quebec who depended on Nova Scotia in the past for their coal supplies will be able to obtain any this year. We were absolutely dependent on the Intercolonial railway for the distribution of coal throughout the Maritime Provinces, with the exception of one or two ports. I am advised that conditions in regard to the supply of what are known as coal cars are very bad. A few days ago the minister told me that about a year ago there had been given to a car company in

my constituency an order for some coal cars which order had not been filled. I have made some inquiries into the matter, and I am advised that the order to which the minister refers was given more than a .year ago, and that it had been filled.
I do not think I said coal cars; I was speaking about box cars.

I was directing the minister's attention then, and I am directing it now to the necessity for the reasons I have indicated, of getting some new coal cars on the Intercolonial. I hope the minister is buying cars liberally for this reason: that last year whatever occurred between the Canadian Pacific and the Intercolonial, the Canadian Pacific would not take freight for transport and delivery to the Intercolonial; in fact complaints came from as far as Newfoundland to that effect. The other day I received a telegram from a friend of mine in business in Newfoundland asking me to see whether some means could not be found for the shipment of some goods which he had ordered in the West, and which of necessity had to go over the Intercolonial to North Sydney to reach Newfoundland, because there is no communication by sea from Montreal. On account of the fact of which the minister is well aware and which I am told is true, that there was some difficulty in regard to the interchange of cars, freight conditions in the Maritime Provinces last winter were such that business men were put to the greatest possible inconvenience. The reason given locally by the railway officials was that cars could not be secured. If that be so, and taking into consideration the fact that extra demands were made upon the railway by reason of the shipment of war supplies, that only accentuates the argument in favour of the minister ordering at once a large number of cars. Over a year ago when the Minister of Customs was putting through the Railway Estimates I urged him to place an order for a supply of cars, and I understand that later on an order was given, but it was given very late in the season, I think, in July.
In May.
We were discussing the matter only about this time last year, and the order was placed after that.
Parliament had prorogued long before this time last year.
Parliament prorogued in the early part of June last year.
In May.

Well, it was in May, just before prorogation that we were discussing the matter. I understood that what the minister referred to was coal cars and not box cars. I would urge him to take steps to ensure that an ample supply of coal cars be obtained for the Intercolonial, and that a supply of box cars is ordered now so that we shall get them within a reasonable time. If we do not order them now, we shall never get them, because there is no telling when the war will stop. It is imperative that the minister should have these cars.

I must have misunderstood the hon. member or he must have misunderstood me. It was box cars that the Eastern Car Company had not delivered on the order given more than a year ago. They sent in a quotation to-day for a number of box cars which they said they would not deliver before March of next year. Therefore, the hon. member can see how hard it is for us to get cars.
The longer you put the matter off the longer the delay.

We are not putting it off, we have given that company an order for a thousand cars which must be filled before the end of the year; we have given an order for another thousand to the Canada Car Company, and we are asking for tenders for 5,000 more. We have scoured the United States for second-hand coal cars in order to help out the situation in the Maritime Provinces; we have secured some, but not as many as we expected. It is almost impossible to get them.

I wish to bring to the notice of the minister the necessity for some improvements at the end of the Intercolonial in connection with my county. The station in my town is absolutely inadequate for the traffic there. It is a small station-house with only one small compartment for a'l kinds of passengers. The minister knows that it is the place where we land passengers for Newfoundland, and he will find, if there is any record kept, that the number of passengers leaving the train at North Sydney is perhaps as large as in any other place with the exception possibly of the city of Halifax.
There are no conveniences at the North Sydney station at all; the accommodation is altogether inadequate for the traffic, and I trust that some steps will soon be taken to give to North Sydney station accommodation commensurate with its needs. As

one of the public, I am sure I may say to the minister that no person in Canada expects the Government Railways to be [DOT]behind the private companies in providing accommodation at stations where the agent whether man or woman, has to stay at night. There is a railway station at a place called McKinnon's Harbour *Much is not fit for a man to live in. This station is in a magnificent farming centre, but 1 suppose the amount of traffic there is not very large. The agent, however, has to stay there summer and winter, and the accommodation is practically, no better than what you would get if you turned a packing case upside down. I should be glad if the minister would provide this agent with accommodation worthy of the railway and of the country. A little farther along the line there is a place called 'Christmas Island, which is quite a traffic centre. Five or six country merchants get their goods at this station, and I am sure the traffic pays well, but there is no accommodation for the goods left at the station and consequently they have to be left on the side of the road with nobody to look after them. Those are three matters that I wish particularly to bring to the attention of the minister because the need is very great, namely, better accommodation for the traffic at North (Sydney and Christmas Island, and reasonable accommodation for the agent who is obliged to live at McKinnon's Harbour. I hope the minister will look into these matters and provide for the accommodation in his estimates next year.	,

\

Have any steps been
taken to take over the Caraquet railway?
