I should like to say a word or two on the subject of (branch lines because it brings prominently before the House the question whether public men are to keep faith with the people of the country, or whether no further attention is to be given to their pledged words. In the latter case we have a condition of affairs that is not calculated to retain the respect and confidence of the people. I think there

have been only two branch lines taken over in the lower provinces. The International railway is a very valuable road, occupying a very important strategic position, and if it were owned by a private company a very large traffic would no doubt be taken away from the Intercolonial.
I think the minister was well advised in carrying out what had been approved of by his predecessor. It has also taken over the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island road. These are the only two. As the minister knows, for years there has been an agitation in this House and throughout the country, in favour of taking over branch lines and operating them as part of the Intercolonial system. As far back as the early fall of 1911, when the general elections campaign was in progress, the hon. member fOT Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler), who is not at present with us as his duties have taken him overseas, was running in a constituency where an intense interest was taken in this question. The people for years had been demanding better accommodation, especially in the county of Gloucester in regard to the Caraquet railway to which my hon. friend has referred. The hon. member for Kings and Albert was exceedingly desirous to give the people to understand that if the Conservative party were returned to power the branch lines would be taken over and made part of the Intercolonial railway. He wired to the leader of the Opposition of that time, the present Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) asking for a telegram clearly defining the policy of the Conservative party on this subject. He received a reply which he deemed entirely satisfactory and which, unfortunately, the people to whom he was appealing also regarded as entirely satisfactory. The words of that telegram from the present Prime Minister I do not recall, but the effect of it was that it had always been the policy of the 'Conservative party to take over the branch lines of the Intercolonial railway. It gave Colonel Fowler clearly to understand that if the Conservatives were honoured with the confidence of the people this policy would be carried into effect. Six years have passed since then, and nothing whatever has yet been done in regard to taking over the railways in that constituency. There are three of them of great importance, the Albert railway, the Elgin and Havelock, and the St. Martins railway. The minister will remember that quite a number of years ago the House unanimously passed a resolution
in favour of taking over the branch lines and making them part of the Intercolonial, and , it has been a great disappointment that nothing whatever has been done in the matter. There are not very many of them and they would be valuable feeders to the Intercolonial, and they would be of infinitely more importance if they were taken over and put into good order so as to operate winter and summer and so that the people could rely upon a continuous and satisfactory service. This ought to appeal to the minister because of the pledged word of the Prime minister which this Government has utterly failed to carry out, greatly to the disappointment of the people. They relied upon the promise, and they are extremely disappointed that it has not been kept. Redress should come from some quarter, though I do not know where it can come from. I feel that if there were a change of government the obligation which this Parliament has taken upon itself in this matter would be fully met. The people despair of getting justice in this matter from this Government, but I think they rely with some confidence upon the pledge if this Parliament being kept, for not only has the Government pledge been given but Parliament also is committed to this policy.
Mr. COCHRANE; I do not know of any time since I became minister when Parliament committed itself to it. Parliament passed a Branch Lines Act, but that does not commit it to the purchasing of all the railways down there. Some of them, as I said once before, instead of being feeders are milkers. There is not any of them but has to be rebuilt, and you could almost build new railways for the same money that it would cost to repair them.

What does the hon.
minister mean by "milkers"? Does he mean that they are like cows that give good milk? It would seem that the Intercolonial takes the milk out of these branches.
I do not think so. We do not interfere with their rates.
You take it out of the passengers.
Nothing of the kind. This is not a question to bring up in war time, when our expenditure in the war is a million a day.
What about the Highways Bill?
The Highways Bill is proposed for good reason. If the war should cease, we have to have a lot of work for our returned soldiers.
Breaking stone.
Oh, oh.
What about the Quebec and Saguenay which was taken over a long time after the war began?
It was agreed to be purchased before the war.
What about paying the Quebec and Saguenay bond-holders a mil. lion and a half which, it is said, they are not entitled to?
We have not paid them.
You have a Bill to pay them.

I wish to call attention to another matter of the branch lines down home, even if it be war time. It is all very well for the minister to talk about "war time" and say that he cannot build roads now; but he could provide $3,000,000 to spend around the North Pole on what they call the Hudson Bay railway.
Your friend beside you (Mr. Oliver) will defend that.
That does not change the latitude of this work, nor dpes it change the fact that the minister is spending these millions on it.
Both parties were committed to it before I came in.

So they were committed to the branch lines. It is no trouble to the minister to go back on the express policy of both parties with regard to the branch lines, but he must go on building the road from Le Pas to Hudson bay. Both parties may have been committed to that project, but, so far as I am concerned, I am not guilty.
The contract was let before I came in.

That may be, but I am not guilty. There was another agreement made with regard to a road down in my part of the country, which agreement was not lived up to; and I think the time has come when this Government should look into it very seriously and do something to 'make good the loss occasioned to the province of New Brunswick. When these

hon. gentlemen opposite came into power in 1911, they found legislation on the statute book providing for the operation of the so-called Valley railway. Providing it was built under certain terms and conditions, they were to take it over from the province and operate it, paying forty per cent of the gross earnings. - The first thing they did was to change the law in 1912, so that they were able to build the road with seven-degree curves and unfavourable grades. Instead of building the road up to the standard set, they built it much below that standard. There was also legislation under which this road was to be built from a point on the Transcontinental at or near Grand Falls to St. John.
It was to be the outlet for all western transcontinental business coming to the port of St. John. One of the first official acts of this Government was to drop the subsidy on the upper end of the road and make it impossible to make that connection. But, acting on the strength of the promise made by this Parliament before this Government came into power, the Government of New Brunswick of that day entered into the construction of this road and have spent somewhere about $7,000,000-I am not sure as to the exact amount, (but a very large amount. They have got the road built from a very bright little town in my constituency called Centreville, extending southwards and in a few months it will be completed to a point on the Canadian Pacific from which they can get connection with St. John. But it is only a local road, and as a result it has only local traffic. They are only able to run one mixed train one way each day, because that enables them to take care of all the traffic that arises. I submit to the House that the expenditure of this money by the Government of New Brunswick was never justified except upon the theory, and upon the agreement, that it was to become a part of the Transcontinental railway. If this Government had carried out the contract which Parliament had made with the people of New Brunswick, if they had not degraded the road, or allowed their friends in New Brunswick to degrade it, if they had not cancelled the subsidy, if they had built the bridge across the St. John river at Andover and made it possible to get connection with the Transcontinental railway, the province of New Brunswick would have received sufficient from its 40 per cent of the earnings of the road to have fairly paid the interest on the bonds. I find from the Budget speech made in the Legislature of New Brunswick at Frederic-

ton last week that they have figured a deficit of a quarter of a million dollars this coming year in interest over and above their share of the earnings of the road. A quarter of a million dollars is an enormous amount to he taken out of the ordinary revenues of a small province like New Brunswick. It has reached a point when there must be direct taxation upon the people of that province to take care of the interest, all because this Government have not carried out the pledge that was made to the people of New Brunswick by virtue of the legislation which they found in existence when they came into power. It is true that they have taken over the operation of the road on an agreement that practically means that 40 per cent goes to the province. But unless they carry out the trade that was made by Parliament in its spirit as well as in its letter and build that road through to the Transcontinental railway, or assist to carry it through by renewing the subsidy which they cut off, unless they stand by the trade in such a way as to enable it to be made a through line, ft is the duty of the Government to take over the road, take over the bonds, pay them and relieve the province of New Brunswick of the enormous drain that they have upon their public revenue. I do not see, in view of the action of the present Government, anything to do but to assume the payment of these bonds, and, of course, take over the road and run it as a part of the Intercolonial.
I am bringing this matter to the minister's attention in the greatest sincerity. I am pointing out how he and his friends have created the condition that exists today. I am not blaming the minister personally at all but I am blaming his Government and their friends for the very unfortunate condition in which we find ourselves to-night. Unless he will in some way get this road through to the Transcontinental and put it where it will get through business, I see nothing in the world to do but take the road over, assume the bonds and run it as a part of the Intercolonial. I hope the minister will give this very serious consideration and I can assure him that no matter what Government is in power in Canada, or what Government is in power in New Brunswick, this is a question which must be faced. I think this is the first time that it has been brought to the attention of this House but it will come up again because the condition is such that it is simply intolerable, all due to the fact that the Government have not carried out
the pledge made to the province and which has forced upon the province an expenditure of $7,000,000 or $8,000,000.

You have absolutely repealed the subsidy from Andover.
Mr. COCHRANE- No, it lapsed; it was not repealed.
It was not renewed.

I know it was not renewed because they have not been able to build the road. We are now living up to our agreement and paying them 40 per cent of the earnings. We have not built the bridge across the river at Andover but
You will not carry out your agreement.
It is impracticable to build it.
Then you refuse to carry out the agreement of Parliament.

I know, but there is common sense in all things and there are things that the Government should do and things they should not do. You know as well as I do that there would not be any traffic over that bridge which would cost' I do not know how much-

It would not cost more than a quarter of a million dollars.
Mr. COCHRANE. A quarter of a million vour granny; you could not touch that for a quarter of a million.
My hon'. friend is talking about something that he does not know anything ab.out.
I know the best engineers in the country think that.

My |hon. friend has
never seen the location of the bridge.

It would not make
any difference if 1 had; I am not giving my own opinion,.

speaking on the reports of any engineers.

Yes, I am. The chief engineer of the old Government appoiniea

for the building of the Quebec bridge made a report in which he said that it would cost $3,000,000.
I knew my hon. friend did not know what he was talking about. He is not talking about the bridge I aim talking about.

You are talking about the bridge across the St. John river?
' Mr. CARVELL: Certainly-at Andover. Mr. COCHRANE: Oh, well.
I knew my hon. friend was not listening to me.

It is the bridge across the river to go to St. John that I am talking about.
Mr. 'CARVELL: I am not talking about that at all. The original proposition was to construct three bridges of which one is at St. John and one at Andover. The bridge at Andover would not cost more than a quarter of a million and I think it might not cost more than $200,000. It would be necessary to make connection with the Transcontinental near Grand Falls. It is an altogether different bridge from the one the minister is talking about?
Yes.

I am not finding any fault in regard t;o that matter because the Government are making connections with St. John, although I do not think it was the best arrangement to make. They are making connection by Westfield and using a portion of the tracks of the Canadian Piacific. But I do find fault that in the .other case they have stopped simply in the country and that they have refused to renew the subsidy from Andover to Grand Falls although they renewed the subsidy from Andover South. In spite of the fact that the department agreed to build that road and have the money all voted for building the road across the St. John river at Andover, the minister has refused. That is why I say he has refused to carry out the trade made between this Parliament and the people of New Brunswick. If he will not carry out this trade upon which we have invested $7,000,000 on a line which is not productive, it is the duty of the minister to take over the bonds, pay the interest, take .over the road, operate the line himself and not compel the people of New Brunswick to pay a quarter of a million dollars interest which we would not have been called upon to pay if we had not had

Mr. Chairman, I am
very glad that my hon. friend from Carle-ton (Mr. Carvell) has called the .attention of the minister to this matter. It is certainly one of very great importance. I aim able to corroborate all that has -been said because I was a member pf the Government which arranged for the original subsidy all the way from Grand Falls to St. John.
Delegations came from New Brunswick, representing the Provincial Government, boards of trade, and other important interests, and the whole idea was based upon connection with the Transcontinental railway at Grand Falls. If it had not been for that, I should not have asked my colleagues nor the people representing New Brunswick, to engage in the enterprise at all. It was only by reason of the road being part of the National Transcontinental railway that the matter could be justified. A subsidy was granted originally on the road from Grand Falls to St. John. The hon. gentleman from Carleton has said very truly that different connection has been made from Gagetown to St. John from that which was originally contemplated. Perhaps that may work out fairly well, but certainly not so well as if the original project had been carried out. It leaves the upper end simply terminating in a prosperous village, but having no connection with the Transcontinental system. The minister is entirely in error when he says the company failed to complete the road, and that the subsidy from Andover to Grand Falls lapsed. The company had the road under construction when this Parliament was asked by the minister to repeal that portion of the subsidy which applied to the section from Andover to Grand1 Falls. There was no failure on the part of the company. The subsidy had not lapsed, and if the minister will refer to the statute he will find a new subsidy from Andover to Grand Falls was substituted for the one from St. John to Grand Falls, and none of us could understand why it was left out. There must have been some Ethiopian in the woodpile, and just what it was I do not know.
We all protested.

Yes. And the late Premier Flemming went up to Grand Falls, and told us that it was going to be built, notwithstanding the fact that the minister himself had induced Parliament' to alter the statute by repealing the provision for [DOT] a subsidy from Grand Falls to St. John

and substituting a subsidy from Andover to St. John.

I want to place before the committee the position in regard to certain railways in the West, to which I made allusion a few minutes ago. I noticed the minister's remark that a time of war was not a time to consider the building of railways. In the instance I wish to mention, I think I can prove to him that the time of war is the time these roads should be completed, because this is the time when we desire to increase production, and people are settling in these districts depending upon the completion of these railroads for the increase of production.
To what roads do you refer,?

Canadian Northern, the line northwesterly from Edmonton and the line northeasterly from Edmonton. Those districts are occupied by a large number of people who have been retarded in the development of their land by reason of the lack of railway communication, but when the road was graded from Edmonton to White Court, in 1913, it was universally taken for granted that the establishment of railway facilities was only a matter of another year. The people who were already in the country were encouraged, and other people went into the country and established themselves there, and the operations of those people have been at a standstill ever since, on account of the road not being completed. The grade is there for over fifty miles from the present terminus, at the crossing of the Pembina river, to White Court, and the grading is going out of repair. It was almost completed ready for the rails, and very expensive work had been done on it. Large cuttings and large trestle works have been put in. The St. Paul de Metis road is directed towards a settlement, some of the settlers in which are 120 miles from the road to-day. Those settlers went into that large tract of country a number of years ago. The district is fertile and attractive. The people are enterprising, but it is impossible for those people to increase their production at such a distance from the railroad. These railroads were chartered originally by the provincial government. They are built under provincial government charter, and aid was given the Canadian Northern Railway Company by provincial government guarantee. The bonds guaranteed by the provincial government
were sold by the railway company to cover one hundred miles on the St. Paul de Metis branch, and about the same on the White Court branch, and construction was begun on the St. Paul de Metis branch, The grade was completed on the White Court branch for a distance of 130 miles from Edmonton. Later on steel was laid on the White Court branch for 70 miles from Edmonton, and no steel was laid for some years on the St. Paul de Metis branch, but recently the grade on the St. Paul de Metis branch was completed for 100 miles, and it is understood 50 miles of steel is now being laid, leaving 50 miles yet to be covered by the steel. When the $45,000,000 guarantee was given to the Canadian Northern, security was taken by this Government on the Canadian Northern western branch lines, and the money raised on the bonds guaranteed by the provincial government appeared in the statement of the assets of the Canadian Northern as security to this Government for the guarantee of $45,000,000. The conditions of the guarantee were that these properties were mortgaged to this Government by second mortgage. The provincial government, which gave the guarantee held a first mortgage on the properties. The second mortgage held by the Dominion Government acted as a bar to the railway company raising any more money, because the money could not be raised in the face of the mortgage to the Dominion Government, and their enterprise has been stalled in that condition ever since, and for that reason this Gov-r eminent, in order to protect its second mortgage, paid the interest on the bond guaranteed by the provincial government and sold by the company. If the interest were not paid, the road would become the property of the provincial government under their first mortgage. In that way, the Dominion Government becomes responsible for the construction of these roads, and still the roads are not completed and have no earning power. I have brought the matter to the attention of the House during previous sessions, and have urged that, under the circumstances, the Government having made itself responsible for the interest on the bonds, they should complete the railway so that it may be able to earn the bond interest. If these roads were completed to White Court in one case, and 100 miles toward St. Paul de Metis in the other case, it would add enormously to the productiveness of that part of the country, in which population is already established,

but is unable to increase its production because of lack of railway facilities. Money employed to secure the completion of these railroads would not be money diverted from the purpose of winning the war; it would rather be money well spent for the purpose of increasiing the production that is necessary to win the war. My hon. friend's Government has money with which to buy and to bonus railroads in other parts of Canada. If it was necessary to put up money to the extent of the ordinary aid given to a railway company in order to complete these roads, no precedent would be broken. It would be doing no more for the people in the part of t'he country affected than is done for people in every other part of the country. I urge upon the minister the desirability of the Government's taking steps to put these railroads in a position to earn interest on their bonds and to secure largely increased production at the hands of people who are settled along those lines and who are discouraged by the disappointment that they have suffered through the non-completion of the roads, the construction of which was their inducement to occupy the lands.

We have heard a good deal to-night about what the Government are doing in other provinces; about their building and bonusing railways in other parts of Canada. That phrase " other parts of Canada " has been referred to so often that I do not think that it should pass unchallenged. Only a few years ago hon. gentlemen who are now advocating the Government's doing something for their respective provinces strenuously objected to the payment of the usual subsidy to a railroad in Ontario which the Provincial Government itself undertook to build and pay for. The members for Edmonton and St. John were members of that Government. Year after year the Provincial Government made application for the subsidy. We remember the strenuous opposition that was made when this Government took steps in the matter; how the Bill was finally passed and then rejected by the Senate; how it was passed again the next year and approved by the Senate by only a narrow majority. I do not like to hear so much about " other parts of Canada."
I think that the province of Ontario applied for the Dominion subsidy after the road was built. The road was undef construction long before application for subsidy was made to this Government.
I am quite positive that time and again application was made to the Government in power at that time for the subsidy, and that it was as often refused.
Does my hon. friend say that application was made by the Ross Government?
Yes.
I do not think so.

The late Hon. Sir George Ross himself is on record to that effect. The member for St. John says that the Government ought to take over and operate certain roads in the eastern provinces. We all remember the position taken by hon. gentlemen opposite last year when the province of Ontario objected to the renewing of a charter to an outside company, in view of the fact that the province itself was willing to build without asking this Government for a dollar. Yet hon. gentlemen in this committee and elsewhere strenuously opposed the attitude of the Ontario Government. The Government desire to be consistent; they desire to deal with all provinces alike. They cannot single out New Brunswick and extend to that province concessions which are not extended to other provinces. I think the time has passed when arguments of that nature should be made in the House.

What does the hon.
gentleman say about the Quebec and Saguenay railway?

Year after year, discussing the branch lines in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, hon. gentlemen told us the same story. In the case to which I refer, they were opposed to the granting of the usual Government subsidy of $6,400 a mile, although the Ontario Government were themselves building the road. No . company would build it, because of the view that the undertaking would not be profitable. That shows the difference in the conditions existing in the several provinces

I would suggest that we let this item stand-the late Minister of Railways is absent; he would, perhaps, like to speak on this item-and pass items 104, 105, and 106. The minister has made good progress in the way of getting the ideas of the members-which is almost as good as getting votes through, because discussion must take place.

I accept my hon.
friend's suggestion.
The member for Richmond might later desire to say something on item 106. There will be no objection to that?

No.
